position: both — mostly after a verb: *His shirt was untucked*

senses.gloss: Of a shirt: hanging loose instead of being tucked into pants or a skirt.
examples: He showed up in jeans and an *untucked* shirt.
Your shirt is *untucked* in the back.
The dress code says no *untucked* shirts.

senses.gloss: Not able to be used, because it is broken, damaged or badly made.
examples: The flood left the whole first floor *unusable*.
Without a charger the laptop is *unusable*.
Half the seats have such a bad view that they're basically *unusable*.

position: both — *unused to* only after a verb
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing* in the sense 'not accustomed' (*unused to the heat*, *unused to being alone*)
contrast: Two words share one spelling. *Unused* 'not used' ends in a z sound, uhn-YOOZD; *unused to* 'not accustomed to' ends in an s sound, uhn-YOOST, like *used to*. After *unused to* comes a noun or *-ing*, never a bare verb: *unused to working nights*.

senses.gloss: Not used; still new, or never taken advantage of.
examples: She has three weeks of *unused* vacation.
The back bedroom sits *unused* most of the year.
Return any *unused* portion for a refund.

senses.gloss: unused to: not accustomed to something.
examples: *Unused* to the cold, he wore two jackets.
She was *unused* to being interrupted.

takes: *for* + noun with a *to*-infinitive (*It's unusual for her to be late*)

senses.gloss: Not normal or common; different from what you expect.
examples: It's *unusual* for him to call this late.
She has an *unusual* name.
There was nothing *unusual* about the car.

contrast: With *the* and no noun it becomes a group noun: *the unvaccinated*.

senses.gloss: Not having been given a vaccine against a disease.
examples: *Unvaccinated* children can't enroll until the fall.
He's still *unvaccinated* against the flu.
The clinic tracks how many patients remain *unvaccinated*.

position: both — mostly before a noun in the 'plain' sense

senses.gloss: Plain and honest, with nothing softened or left out.
examples: He gave us the *unvarnished* truth.
I want your *unvarnished* opinion, not the polite version.

senses.gloss: Not covered with varnish.
examples: The shelves are *unvarnished* pine.
We left the floor *unvarnished* on purpose.

senses.gloss: Impossible to check or prove true.
examples: The whole story rests on *unverifiable* claims.
Most of what he posted online is *unverifiable*.
Anonymous tips are often *unverifiable*.

contrast: *Unverified* means nobody has checked it yet; *unverifiable* means it cannot be checked at all.

senses.gloss: Not yet checked or confirmed.
examples: *Unverified* reports say the plant is closing.
The number is still *unverified*.
Please don't pass along *unverified* information.

senses.gloss: Not wanted or welcome.
examples: The drug has some *unwanted* side effects.
She was getting a lot of *unwanted* attention at work.
Drop off any *unwanted* clothes by Friday.

senses.gloss: Not justified by the facts or by the situation.
examples: The criticism was completely *unwarranted*.
He called the search an *unwarranted* invasion of privacy.
Their fear turned out to be *unwarranted*.

contrast: Mostly written, in phrases like *the unwary buyer* or *a trap for the unwary*. In speech Americans say *careless* or *not paying attention*.

senses.gloss: Not watching out for danger or for a trick.
examples: The scam targets *unwary* shoppers.
*Unwary* hikers sometimes walk right past the trailhead.
Small print like that is written for the *unwary* customer.

contrast: *The great unwashed* is an old, snobbish way of saying 'ordinary people' — there the word is a noun, not the adjective.

senses.gloss: Not washed; still dirty.
examples: Don't eat *unwashed* berries.
A pile of *unwashed* dishes filled the sink.
His hair was *unwashed* and sticking up in back.

senses.gloss: Staying firm and steady; never weakening or changing.
examples: She has had his *unwavering* support from day one.
He kept an *unwavering* focus on the goal.
Her loyalty to the team was *unwavering*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an unwed mother*
contrast: Formal and somewhat dated, mostly in *unwed mother* and in legal writing. Everyday American English says *single* or *unmarried*.

senses.gloss: Not married.
examples: The article was about *unwed* mothers in the 1950s.
The form asks whether the parents were *unwed* at the time of the birth.
*Unwed* couples weren't eligible for the benefit back then.

senses.gloss: Not wanted; causing unhappiness or discomfort.
examples: The bill came as an *unwelcome* surprise.
They made her feel *unwelcome* at the meeting.
It was *unwelcome* news for investors.

position: predicative only — *She felt unwell*; before a noun use *sick*
contrast: Formal and softer than *sick*. Americans normally say *I'm sick* or *I don't feel good*; *unwell* belongs to notes, news and polite speech. It never goes before a noun: *a sick child*, not *an unwell child*.

senses.gloss: Slightly ill; not feeling healthy.
examples: She went home early because she felt *unwell*.
He's been *unwell* for several weeks.
If you are *unwell*, please stay home.

senses.gloss: Bad for your health, your mind or your character.
examples: The diet was cheap but *unwholesome*.
They worried about the *unwholesome* influence of his new friends.
There was something *unwholesome* about the whole arrangement.

senses.gloss: Big or awkward, and therefore hard to carry, move or handle.
examples: The mattress was *unwieldy* on the stairs.
He wrestled the *unwieldy* box into the trunk.

senses.gloss: Too large or too complicated to work well.
examples: The committee has grown *unwieldy* — twenty-two members now.
The tax rules are so *unwieldy* that nobody reads them.

senses.gloss: Not sensible; likely to lead to trouble.
examples: It would be *unwise* to sign anything today.
Borrowing that much was an *unwise* move.
He made a few *unwise* decisions early in his career.

contrast: The adverb *unwittingly* is far more common: *He unwittingly helped them*. The adjective says the person had no idea what they were part of, not that they were careless.

senses.gloss: Not knowing what is really going on; doing something without meaning to.
examples: He became an *unwitting* accomplice in the scheme.
The *unwitting* customers paid the fee twice.
She was an *unwitting* participant in the study.

senses.gloss: Impossible to carry out or to make work in practice.
examples: The plan turned out to be *unworkable*.
They rejected it as an *unworkable* compromise.
Without more staff, the schedule is *unworkable*.

senses.gloss: Not experienced in practical life; not interested in money or status.
examples: He was a gentle, *unworldly* man who never locked his door.
She seemed *unworldly* for someone who had traveled so much.
They lead a quiet, *unworldly* life on the farm.

position: both — mostly after a verb with *of*

senses.gloss: Not deserving something; not good enough for it.
examples: He felt *unworthy* of such praise.
That kind of behavior is *unworthy* of a judge.
She dismissed the rumor as *unworthy* of comment.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an unwritten rule*

senses.gloss: Not written down, but understood and followed anyway.
examples: There's an *unwritten* rule about taking the last slice.
The agreement was *unwritten*, but everyone honored it.
*Unwritten* office etiquette takes a while to learn.

senses.gloss: Not yet written.
examples: The last chapter of the story is still *unwritten*.
Their future is *unwritten*.

senses.gloss: Refusing to change your mind or give in.
examples: The landlord was *unyielding* about the rent.
Their position on the deadline has been *unyielding*.

senses.gloss: Hard and not bending under weight or pressure.
examples: The mattress was thin and *unyielding*.
Concrete floors are *unyielding* on your knees.

position: both — mostly after a verb (*Sales are up*); before a noun only in fixed uses: *the up escalator*, *an up year*
contrast: *Up* is usually an adverb or a preposition (*stand up*, *up the stairs*). It counts as an adjective when it follows *be*, *get* or *seem*: *The market is up*, *Are you up?* Before a noun it is rare and fixed.

senses.gloss: Higher than before in amount, level or price.
examples: Sales are *up* eight percent this quarter.
Gas prices are *up* again.
Attendance was *up* from last year.

senses.gloss: Awake and out of bed.
examples: I was *up* at five this morning.
Are the kids *up* yet?

senses.gloss: Working; running normally.
examples: The server is back *up*.
The site should be *up* again by noon.

senses.gloss: Finished, of a period of time.
examples: Time's *up*!
Your thirty days are *up* on Friday.

contrast: Only the idiom is an adjective; *The kite is up in the air* is literal. It means 'not decided yet', not 'in doubt about quality'.

senses.gloss: Not decided or settled yet.
examples: Our vacation plans are still *up in the air*.
Whether they'll move is *up in the air*.
The whole schedule was left *up in the air* after the storm.

takes: a noun or pronoun (*up to you*, *up to the job*); *-ing* (*up to driving*)
contrast: *Up to* is also a quantity word meaning 'as many as' (*up to fifty people*) and part of verbs like *keep up to date*. As an adjective it follows *be*: *It's up to you*, *He's up to something*, *I'm not up to it today*.

senses.gloss: up to someone: that person's decision or responsibility.
examples: It's *up to* you where we eat.
Whether we go is *up to* the weather.
It's *up to* the manager to approve the refund.

senses.gloss: Doing something secret, usually something you shouldn't.
examples: What are those two *up to*?
He's *up to* something — he's been way too quiet.

senses.gloss: Well enough or good enough for something.
examples: I don't feel *up to* going out tonight.
He just isn't *up to* the job.

form: compound — always hyphenated before a noun

senses.gloss: Becoming successful or popular, and likely to do even better soon.
examples: She's an *up-and-coming* chef with two restaurants already.
The neighborhood is full of *up-and-coming* little places.
The label signs *up-and-coming* bands.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun, often open after a verb
form: compound — preposition phrase used as one adjective
contrast: *Up-to-date* is the broader word (not out of date); *up-to-the-minute* stresses that nothing newer exists.

senses.gloss: Including the very latest information.
examples: The app gives you *up-to-the-minute* traffic.
We need *up-to-the-minute* numbers before the call.
Their storm coverage is *up-to-the-minute*.

contrast: The noun *upbeat* is a musical term; the adjective is about mood. *Upbeat* is about how something sounds or feels; *optimistic* is about expecting good results.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and positive in mood or tone.
examples: The song has an *upbeat* tempo.
She stayed *upbeat* through the whole ordeal.
The report ends on an *upbeat* note.

position: attributive only — *the upcoming election*; after a verb say *coming up*

senses.gloss: Happening soon.
examples: Tickets for the *upcoming* season go on sale Monday.
We spent the meeting on the *upcoming* election.
Watch your email for our *upcoming* events.

senses.gloss: Turned over so that the wrong end or side is up.
examples: An *upended* canoe lay on the bank.
The chairs sat *upended* on the tables.
We found the trash cans *upended* after the storm.

takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* in the 'honest' sense (*upfront about the cost*)
contrast: Also written *up-front*. The money sense is often an adverb, two words: *You pay $500 up front*.

senses.gloss: Paid or given before anything else happens.
examples: There's a $200 *upfront* fee.
The *upfront* cost is high, but you save later.

senses.gloss: Honest and direct about what you think or about the facts.
examples: She was *upfront* about the risks.
I'll be *upfront* with you: this is going to take months.

ru: идущий в гору; тяжёлый, требующий больших усилий
position: attributive only — after a verb *uphill* is an adverb: *The road runs uphill*

senses.gloss: Going up a slope.
examples: The last mile is a steep *uphill* climb.
We took the *uphill* route on purpose.

senses.gloss: Difficult and needing long, hard effort.
examples: They face an *uphill* battle in court.
Getting funding has been an *uphill* fight from the start.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *an upper-class family*
contrast: The noun is two words with no hyphen: *the upper class*. In American English the label is about money and family, not about accent.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the richest and highest social class.
examples: He grew up in an *upper-class* suburb.
The novel makes fun of *upper-class* manners.
Her background is solidly *upper-class*.

senses.gloss: More advanced, of college courses.
examples: You need two *upper-level* electives to graduate.
*Upper-level* classes are much smaller.

senses.gloss: Senior; near the top of an organization.
examples: The memo went to *upper-level* management.
*Upper-level* officials refused to comment.

form: compound — three words joined by hyphens

senses.gloss: Belonging to the wealthier part of the middle class.
senses.ru: принадлежащий к верхней части среднего класса
examples: They live in a quiet *upper-middle-class* neighborhood.
The show is about *upper-middle-class* parents in the suburbs.
By any measure the family was *upper-middle-class*.

contrast: Everyday speech says *capital letters*; *uppercase* belongs to typing, printing and password rules. Also written *upper-case*.

senses.gloss: Written as a capital letter.
examples: Type your last name in *uppercase* letters.
The first character has to be *uppercase*.
The sign was printed in *uppercase* type.

position: both — the 'in someone's mind' sense only after a verb

senses.gloss: Highest in position.
examples: A few leaves still clung to the *uppermost* branches.
Keep the heavy pans out of the *uppermost* cabinet.

senses.gloss: Most important in someone's thoughts.
examples: Safety was *uppermost* in her mind.
One question was *uppermost*: who paid for all this?

contrast: Informal and disapproving: it says someone is acting above the place others assign them. In the United States it carries an ugly history of being used about Black people who refused to defer, so it is a word to recognize rather than to use.

senses.gloss: Acting as if you are more important than others think you are.
examples: He got *uppity* with the manager and was asked to leave.
They called her *uppity* for speaking her mind.
There's an *uppity* tone to the whole letter.

contrast: *Upright* is also an adverb (*sit upright*) and a noun (*an upright*, meaning a piano or a post).

senses.gloss: Standing straight up; vertical.
examples: Please put your seat back in the *upright* position.
Keep the box *upright* so nothing spills.

senses.gloss: Honest and behaving by the rules.
examples: He had a reputation as an *upright* citizen.
She's the most *upright* person I know.

senses.gloss: Extremely funny.
examples: The second act is *uproarious*.
He told an *uproarious* story about his first day on the job.

senses.gloss: Very noisy and full of loud laughter.
examples: The joke was met with *uproarious* laughter.
The party got *uproarious* around midnight.

contrast: An American word; British English says *upmarket*.

senses.gloss: Expensive and aimed at people with money.
examples: They opened an *upscale* steakhouse downtown.
The neighborhood has gotten much more *upscale*.
It's an *upscale* hotel, with prices to match.

contrast: *Upsetting* news makes you feel bad; an *upset* person already feels bad: *The letter was upsetting* / *She was upset*.

senses.gloss: Making someone feel unhappy, worried or angry.
examples: The video is *upsetting* to watch.
It was an *upsetting* thing to hear from your own doctor.
The most *upsetting* part was that nobody called us.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun (*an upside-down cake*), usually two words after a verb (*The picture is upside down*)
contrast: Also an adverb: *You're holding it upside down*. The idiom *turn something upside down* means to search it or disturb it completely.

senses.gloss: With the top part at the bottom.
examples: The map was *upside-down*.
She made an *upside-down* pineapple cake.
One of the photos got scanned *upside-down*.

contrast: Most of the time *upstairs* is an adverb (*go upstairs*) or a noun (*the whole upstairs*). Only before a noun is it an adjective.

senses.gloss: Located on an upper floor.
examples: The *upstairs* bathroom is being redone.
We rented out the *upstairs* apartment.
Their *upstairs* neighbors play music all night.

contrast: Almost always in *an upstanding citizen* or *an upstanding member of the community*; it can sound formal or lightly ironic.

senses.gloss: Honest and respectable.
examples: He's an *upstanding* member of the community.
The defense called her hardworking and *upstanding*.
They seemed like *upstanding* people.

contrast: Mostly a noun: *He's an upstart* (выскочка). Before another noun it means 'new and pushing in where nobody expected it', usually with a hint of disapproval.

senses.gloss: New and ambitious, and challenging those already established.
examples: An *upstart* airline is undercutting the majors.
The *upstart* candidate finished a close second.
*Upstart* studios are taking market share from the big ones.

ru: расположенный выше по течению; начальный (в производственной цепочке)
position: attributive only — after a verb it is an adverb: *The dam is two miles upstream*

senses.gloss: Closer to the source of a river.
examples: *Upstream* towns get their water first.
The *upstream* side of the dam has silted up.

senses.gloss: At an early stage of a process or a supply chain.
examples: The company sold off its *upstream* oil operations.
An *upstream* supplier missed a deadline and the whole line stopped.

contrast: Informal. It mixes anxiety with being too strict or easily shocked, so *Don't be so uptight* means 'relax, stop making rules'.

senses.gloss: Nervous and tense, often about small things, and unable to relax.
examples: He gets *uptight* about being on time.
Don't be so *uptight* — it's just a game.
She's the most *uptight* person in the office.

contrast: American usage: in New York *uptown* is the northern part of Manhattan; in many other cities it is the residential part away from the business district. It is also an adverb (*We're heading uptown*) and a noun.

senses.gloss: In or belonging to the uptown part of a city.
examples: They have an *uptown* apartment near the park.
The *uptown* train is running late.
It was an *uptown* crowd in expensive coats.

position: attributive only — mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Turned or pointing upward.
examples: She has a small *upturned* nose.
A row of *upturned* faces watched the balloon.

senses.gloss: Turned upside down.
examples: He sat on an *upturned* bucket.
*Upturned* boats lined the beach.

contrast: The adjective is always *upward*; the adverb can be *upward* or *upwards* (*prices moved upward*, *upwards*). Never write *an upwards trend*.

senses.gloss: Moving or pointing toward a higher level.
examples: Home prices are on an *upward* trend.
There's *upward* pressure on wages.
The chart shows a steady *upward* climb since March.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is an adverb: *Stay upwind*

senses.gloss: On the side that the wind is coming from.
examples: Take the *upwind* side of the fire.
The *upwind* boats had the advantage.
Smoke never reaches the *upwind* end of the camp.

contrast: *Urban* means 'of the city'; *urbane* means 'polished and sophisticated'. Different words, different stress: UR-buhn and ur-BAYN.

senses.gloss: Relating to a city or to city life.
examples: *Urban* schools face different problems than rural ones.
The county gets more *urban* every year.
She studies *urban* planning.

contrast: Not a synonym of *urban*: an *urbane* host is smooth and well-mannered, not 'from the city'.

senses.gloss: Polite, confident and at ease socially, in a way that suggests wide experience.
examples: He was an *urbane* host who put everyone at ease.
Her writing is witty and *urbane*.
The ambassador is charming and *urbane*.

takes: *that*-clause with the base verb (*It's urgent that she call us*)
contrast: Russian *срочный* can also mean 'fast': an order that has to be filled quickly is a *rush order* or *express delivery*, not an *urgent delivery*.

senses.gloss: Needing to be dealt with right away.
examples: I got an *urgent* message from the school.
This is more *urgent* than the budget report.
Nothing on the list is *urgent*.

senses.gloss: Showing that you want something done at once.
examples: There was an *urgent* note in her voice.
He made an *urgent* appeal for volunteers.

senses.gloss: Relating to urine and the organs that make and carry it.
examples: She's being treated for a *urinary* tract infection.
The *urinary* system includes the kidneys and the bladder.
*Urinary* problems are common after this surgery.

contrast: Always capitalized. The same word is a noun for a person (*two Uruguayans*); the country is *Uruguay*.

senses.gloss: From Uruguay, or relating to Uruguay.
examples: We went to a *Uruguayan* steakhouse.
The *Uruguayan* team won on penalties.
Her grandparents are *Uruguayan*.

contrast: The American spelling is *usable*; *useable* is a rarer variant. Note the z sound, YOO-zuh-buhl, though the noun *use* ends in an s sound.

senses.gloss: In good enough condition to be used.
examples: Only half the field is *usable* after the rain.
Is any of this lumber still *usable*?

senses.gloss: Easy to use, of software, tools and designs.
examples: The new site is far more *usable* on a phone.
They redesigned the app to make it *usable* for beginners.

takes: *to* + noun, pronoun or *-ing* (*used to the noise*, *used to getting up early*)
contrast: Two different things share this spelling. *Be* or *get used to* + noun or *-ing* means 'be accustomed to' (привык): *I'm used to working nights*. *Used to* + a bare verb is a past habit and never has *be*: *I used to work nights* (раньше работал). The classic mistake is *I'm used to work here* — say *I'm used to working here* or *I used to work here*. Both are pronounced with an s sound: YOOST.

senses.gloss: Familiar with something because you have done it or had it often.
examples: I'm *used to* the noise now.
It takes about a week to get *used to* the altitude.
She isn't *used to* driving in snow.

takes: *for* + noun or *-ing*; *to* + a person; *to*-infinitive (*useful to know*)

senses.gloss: Helpful for doing or getting something.
examples: That's a *useful* tip, thanks.
A second key would be *useful* for the neighbors.
It's *useful* to know a little Spanish around here.

takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* in the informal 'bad at' sense (*useless at math*)

senses.gloss: Not useful; of no help at all.
examples: A phone with no signal is *useless*.
It's *useless* to argue with him.
These old batteries are *useless*.

senses.gloss: Very bad at doing something — informal.
examples: I'm *useless* at remembering names.
He's *useless* in the kitchen.

ru: удобный для пользователя, простой в обращении

senses.gloss: Easy to use or understand, especially for people who are not experts.
examples: The new dashboard is much more *user-friendly*.
We need a *user-friendly* version of the manual.
Their checkout process isn't very *user-friendly*.

position: both — mostly before a noun; after a verb usually with *it*: *It's usual to tip*
takes: *for* + noun with a *to*-infinitive (*It's usual for guests to bring something*)
contrast: *As usual* is fixed (*He was late, as usual*), and *the usual* is a noun (*I'll have the usual*). Don't mix the adjective *usual* with the adverb *usually*: *my usual seat* / *I usually sit here*.

senses.gloss: Happening or done most of the time; normal for this person or situation.
examples: We met at our *usual* table.
It's *usual* to tip about twenty percent.
She took the *usual* route home.

contrast: Formal, mostly legal and financial. The noun is *usury*, YOO-zhuh-ree: lending money at illegally high interest.

senses.gloss: Charging interest at an unfairly or illegally high rate.
examples: The lawsuit calls the fees *usurious*.
Payday lenders charge *usurious* rates.
The contract was thrown out as *usurious*.

senses.gloss: Made to be useful rather than attractive.
examples: The kitchen is plain and *utilitarian*.
They chose *utilitarian* furniture that could take a beating.

senses.gloss: Relating to utilitarianism, the idea that the right action brings the most good to the most people.
examples: He made a *utilitarian* argument for the policy.
The debate turned into a cold *utilitarian* calculation.

contrast: In *utility bill*, *utility company* and *utility room* this is the noun *utility* used as a modifier. The adjective proper means 'able to fill several roles' (*a utility infielder*) or 'plain and practical' (*utility shelving*).

senses.gloss: Able to play several positions or do several different jobs.
examples: He's a *utility* infielder who can catch, too.
Every crew needs one *utility* player who can cover anything.

senses.gloss: Made for plain practical use rather than for looks.
examples: We put *utility* shelving in the garage.
It's a *utility* knife, not a fancy one.

contrast: Also a noun: *She did her utmost*. Don't confuse it with *uppermost*, which is about position. The variant *uttermost* is literary.

senses.gloss: The greatest possible — used to stress how much.
examples: This is a matter of the *utmost* importance.
Handle the samples with the *utmost* care.
He has the *utmost* respect for her.

contrast: Capitalized when it points to Thomas More's *Utopia*, lowercase in ordinary use. It usually hints that the plan is too perfect to work.

senses.gloss: Imagining or aiming at a perfect society, often unrealistically.
examples: It's a *utopian* vision with no plan to pay for it.
The commune started out with *utopian* ideals.
Critics called the proposal *utopian*.

contrast: Written with a capital V and a hyphen: *a V-shaped valley*. Economists use it for a downturn that rebounds just as fast as it fell.

senses.gloss: Shaped like the letter V, wide at the top and narrow at the bottom.
examples: The trail follows a *V-shaped* valley.
She wore a sweater with a *V-shaped* neckline.
Geese fly in a *V-shaped* formation.

contrast: *Vacant* means empty and available: a *vacant* room can be taken. *Empty* only says there is nothing in it.

senses.gloss: Empty and available; not occupied.
examples: There's a *vacant* lot behind the store.
Two apartments in the building are *vacant*.

senses.gloss: Of a job or a position: not filled.
examples: The seat has been *vacant* since March.
They're advertising a *vacant* teaching position.

senses.gloss: Showing no thought or interest.
examples: He gave me a *vacant* stare.
Her expression went *vacant* for a second.

senses.gloss: Having been given a vaccine to protect against a disease.
examples: All the kids are fully *vaccinated*.
Are you *vaccinated* against hepatitis?
*Vaccinated* travelers skip the extra paperwork.

senses.gloss: Empty of ideas or meaning; silly.
examples: The speech was polished but *vacuous*.
He asked a string of *vacuous* questions.

senses.gloss: Showing no thought or feeling, of a look or a smile.
examples: She wore a *vacuous* smile the whole time.
His face went *vacuous* when we asked for details.

senses.gloss: Relating to the vagina.
examples: She had a *vaginal* delivery.
The pharmacy stocks several *vaginal* medications.
*Vaginal* infections are usually easy to treat.

takes: *about* + noun or *-ing* when it describes a person (*vague about the details*)

senses.gloss: Not clear or exact; short on detail.
examples: He gave a *vague* answer about the schedule.
Their plans are still pretty *vague*.
The instructions got *vaguer* the further I read.

senses.gloss: Slight; not strong or definite, of a feeling or a memory.
examples: I have a *vague* memory of the house.
She had a *vague* sense that something was wrong.

senses.gloss: Of a person: not giving details, or not thinking clearly.
examples: He was *vague* about where the money went.
She's a little *vague* before her coffee.

position: both — the 'useless' sense only before a noun: *a vain attempt*
contrast: Three homophones: *vain* (тщеславный), *vein* (вена) and *vane* (флюгер). *In vain* means 'without success': *They searched in vain*.

senses.gloss: Too proud of your looks or your abilities.
examples: He's *vain* about his hair.
She's the *vainest* person I know.

senses.gloss: Unsuccessful; producing no result.
examples: It was a *vain* attempt to save the building.
They made one last *vain* effort to reach him by phone.

contrast: Formal or literary; everyday English says *brave*. It is very common in *a valiant effort*, which is usually said of a try that failed.

senses.gloss: Very brave and determined, especially against long odds.
examples: They made a *valiant* effort to keep the store open.
He was *valiant* in the face of a terrible diagnosis.
The firefighters got a medal for their *valiant* work.

takes: *for* + a period or a purpose (*valid for six months*)
contrast: The opposite is stressed in-VAL-id when it means 'not valid'; the noun *invalid*, a person too sick to care for themselves, is stressed IN-vuh-lid.

senses.gloss: Officially or legally acceptable.
examples: You need a *valid* driver's license.
The coupon is *valid* through Sunday.

senses.gloss: Based on good reasoning; fair.
examples: That's a *valid* point.
She had a *valid* reason for missing the exam.

senses.gloss: Officially checked and confirmed.
examples: Only *validated* results go into the report.
The lab uses a *validated* testing method.

senses.gloss: Feeling that your feelings or your experience have been recognized as real.
examples: She felt *validated* when the doctor finally believed her.
It feels good to be *validated* by people you respect.

takes: *to* + a person (*valuable to us*); *for* + noun or *-ing*
contrast: *Invaluable* is not the opposite of *valuable* — it means so useful that no price fits: *Her advice was invaluable*. The plural noun *valuables* means jewelry, money and the like.

senses.gloss: Worth a lot of money.
examples: The ring is quite *valuable*.
Lock your *valuable* equipment in the van.

senses.gloss: Very useful or important.
examples: That was *valuable* advice.
She's the most *valuable* person on the team.

position: both — before a noun in *a valued customer*, after a verb in *feel valued*
contrast: *Valued* means appreciated by people; *valuable* means worth a lot of money. Watch for the verb as well: *a painting valued at $2 million* means someone set that price.

senses.gloss: Treated as important and appreciated.
examples: Thank you for being a *valued* customer.
Employees need to feel *valued*.
He was a *valued* member of the department.

contrast: In *vanilla ice cream* and *vanilla extract* this is the noun, the flavor. As an adjective it is informal and means 'plain, with no special features', usually about products, software or plans.

senses.gloss: Ordinary, with no special features.
examples: It's a pretty *vanilla* setup — nothing custom.
They offered a plain *vanilla* version of the loan.
The movie was *vanilla* but pleasant enough.

contrast: Formal and dismissive, close to *vacuous*, but used more about talk, writing and entertainment than about faces.

senses.gloss: Dull and empty of interest or ideas.
examples: The interview was a string of *vapid* questions.
I couldn't sit through another *vapid* reality show.
Her lyrics are catchy but *vapid*.

contrast: Also a noun in math and science (*solve for the variable*). *Variable* means it changes; *various* means several different ones.

senses.gloss: Likely to change; not staying the same.
examples: The weather here is highly *variable*.
Service has been *variable* at best.

senses.gloss: Able to be set at different levels.
examples: The drill has a *variable* speed setting.
They offer a *variable* interest rate.

position: attributive only — almost always in *varicose veins*

senses.gloss: Of a vein: swollen and twisted, usually in the legs.
examples: She's having her *varicose* veins treated.
*Varicose* veins run in my family.
Standing all day can make *varicose* veins worse.

contrast: *Varied* describes a range that holds many kinds (*a varied menu*); *various* means 'several different' and goes straight before a plural noun (*various reasons*).

senses.gloss: Made up of many different kinds; not all the same.
examples: The menu is more *varied* than it looks.
He's had a long and *varied* career.
Reviews have been *varied*.

position: attributive only — straight before a plural noun: *various reasons*
contrast: *Various* replaces the article: *for various reasons*, never *for a various reason*. It does not follow *be* in everyday English — say *The reasons vary*. And it is not *varied*, which is about a rich range.

senses.gloss: Several different.
examples: We looked at *various* options before deciding.
She's lived in *various* cities over the years.
The delay was caused by *various* problems at the port.

contrast: Nearly fixed in *varying degrees*, *varying amounts* and *varying levels*. For something that keeps changing, use *variable*.

senses.gloss: Different from one case to the next; changing in amount or degree.
examples: The programs work, with *varying* degrees of success.
Students arrive with *varying* levels of preparation.
The pills come in *varying* strengths.

senses.gloss: Relating to the tubes that carry blood in the body or sap in a plant.
examples: He sees a *vascular* surgeon twice a year.
Smoking raises the risk of *vascular* disease.
Ferns are *vascular* plants.

contrast: Very common in *the vast majority* (подавляющее большинство). The comparative forms are rare — most writers say *far vaster* or switch to *huge*.

senses.gloss: Extremely large in area, amount or range.
examples: The *vast* majority of readers never comment.
They crossed a *vast* stretch of desert.
Up close, the canyon felt even *vaster* than in the pictures.

senses.gloss: Built with a high, curved or arched ceiling.
examples: The living room has a *vaulted* ceiling.
We ate under the *vaulted* arches of the old market.
The chapel's *vaulted* roof is the oldest part of the building.

senses.gloss: Of a patient: alive but showing no awareness — in *a vegetative state*.
examples: He was in a *vegetative* state for two years.
Doctors distinguish a *vegetative* state from a coma.

senses.gloss: Of a plant: growing leaves and stems rather than flowers or seeds.
examples: The plant is still in its *vegetative* stage.
*Vegetative* growth slows once the buds open.

contrast: The stress is on the first syllable and the h is silent: VEE-uh-muhnt. The adverb *vehemently* (*He vehemently denied it*) is more common than the adjective.

senses.gloss: Showing strong, forceful feeling, especially in opposition.
examples: She was *vehement* in her denial.
The plan met *vehement* opposition from the neighbors.
He made a *vehement* argument against the merger.

contrast: Formal, mostly traffic and legal language: *vehicular traffic*, *vehicular homicide*. In ordinary speech say *car* or *traffic*.

senses.gloss: Relating to vehicles, especially cars and trucks.
examples: The bridge is closed to *vehicular* traffic.
He was charged with *vehicular* manslaughter.
*Vehicular* access is from the alley.

position: both — mostly before a noun in the 'hidden' sense
contrast: Very common in *thinly veiled*, which means the hint is obvious to everyone: *a thinly veiled threat*.

senses.gloss: Hinted at rather than said openly.
examples: The email contained a thinly *veiled* threat.
She made a *veiled* reference to his drinking.

senses.gloss: Covered with a veil or a thin layer.
examples: The bride's face was *veiled*.
The mountains were *veiled* in fog.

senses.gloss: Soft and smooth like velvet — of a texture, a voice or a taste.
examples: The petals have a *velvety* feel.
He has a deep, *velvety* voice.
The soup was rich and *velvety*.

contrast: Don't confuse *venal* (продажный, берущий взятки) with *venial*, VEE-nee-uhl, which describes a small, forgivable sin. Formal; everyday English says *corrupt* or *on the take*.

senses.gloss: Willing to be bribed; corrupt.
examples: The novel is set in a *venal* city hall.
Reporters exposed a *venal* inspector who signed off on anything.
The whole system is *venal*, from top to bottom.
